b: The four Gospels are our main sources for the life of Jesus, and the first question about any historical source is how close it is to the events. The answer is better than many people expect.

Jesus was crucified about AD 30 or 33. Paul's letters, written in the AD 50s, already contain early Christian creeds and accounts of the Last Supper and the resurrection that he says he "received." Most scholars date Mark to the late 60s, Matthew and Luke to the 70s or 80s, and John to the 90s, though some date them earlier. Even the latest dates fall within the lifetime of people who had known Jesus. Compare that to the main biographies of Alexander the Great, by Arrian and Plutarch, which were written some four hundred years after his death, and which historians nevertheless use.

The Gospels also make a claim about how they came to be. Luke says that he "carefully investigated everything from the beginning" and that he was drawing on those who had been eyewitnesses (Luke 1:3). John ends by saying that the disciple who wrote it was a witness (John 21:24). Peter writes, "we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty" (2 Peter 1:16). The New Testament scholar Richard Bauckham, in a 2006 book, argued that the Gospels preserve eyewitness memory, noting even that the names of people in them match the pattern of names in first-century Palestine.

The accounts differ, as any set of independent witnesses will. Matthew, Mark and Luke tell the same stories in different words and orders, and the differences are sometimes puzzling. But they agree on the main facts, and in several places they record details that were awkward for the early church, such as the disciples' failures and the women as the first witnesses. Historians call this the criterion of embarrassment, the idea that people do not invent things that embarrass them.

None of this proves that everything in them is true, and scholars argue about many details. But it does mean that the Gospels belong to the kind of sources that historians take seriously, and that their claims have to be dealt with.

Everything in Christianity depends on this question. Paul puts it bluntly: "if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith." So it is worth looking at the case for it, and at what skeptics say.

Historians, including many who are not Christians, accept several facts. Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate. Soon afterward his followers sincerely believed that they had seen him alive. They were willing to suffer and some to die for that belief, which changed them from frightened men into public preachers. The earliest account, in 1 Corinthians 15, is a creed that goes back to within a few years of the events, and it lists witnesses, including more than five hundred at once, "most of whom are still living," who could be asked. And two skeptics, James, the brother of Jesus, and Saul of Tarsus, the persecutor of the church, became believers.

The Gospels add that the tomb was empty and that women were the first to find it, which would have been a strange invention in a culture that gave little weight to women's testimony. Even the enemies of the early church seem to have agreed that the tomb was empty, since the story that they spread was that the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11-15).

Explanations offered by those who do not accept the resurrection include that the disciples were hallucinating, that they went to the wrong tomb, that the body was stolen, or that Jesus did not really die. Each has difficulties. Hallucinations are private, not shared by groups and not likely to produce a bodily encounter that includes eating. The swoon theory was effectively refuted in 1835 by the German scholar David Strauss, who was no believer, on the grounds that a half-dead man could not have inspired faith in a conqueror of death. The scholar N. T. Wright, in a 2003 book, argues that no other explanation accounts for the rise of the early church.

A historical argument cannot compel belief, and many scholars remain unpersuaded. But the Christian claim is that this is the best account of the evidence, and that the question remains open for anyone willing to look.
Skeptics point to passages in the Bible that seem to say different things, and every honest reader meets some. A few simple principles help with most of them, and a few remain hard.

The first principle is to read each passage in context, and the second is to ask what the author was doing. Ancient writers did not always follow modern conventions. They often summarized, rearranged material by topic and not by time, and quoted loosely. Two accounts that differ in detail can both be accurate, like two witnesses who each remember different parts of an event. The Gospels' accounts of Easter morning, for example, differ in the number of women and angels, but they agree about the empty tomb and the appearances, and the differences look more like independent testimony than collusion.

One famous case is the death of Judas. Matthew says that Judas hanged himself (Matthew 27:5). Acts says that "he fell headlong and burst open in the middle" (Acts 1:18). Many readers have suggested that both are true: that he hanged himself, and that the body later fell and burst. Whether or not that is right, the two accounts agree that he died by his own hand, in the field bought with the betrayal money, and each emphasizes a different point.

The genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke differ. Some scholars think that one traces the line through Joseph and the other through Mary, and others that one is the legal line to the throne and the other the biological descent. A third kind of difficulty arises from numbers and dates in the Old Testament, where copying errors are possible.

None of these affects any basic teaching. The Bible's central claims are consistent. A helpful attitude is humility: where we cannot reconcile two passages, we can admit it, and wait. The Christian view is that Scripture is truthful, and the existence of puzzles is part of reading an ancient collection, not evidence that it is unreliable.

Christians live alongside people of other faiths, and the two that are closest historically are Judaism and Islam. A short lesson cannot do justice to either, but a few facts help with respect and with understanding.

Judaism is the faith out of which Christianity grew. Jesus, his disciples and Paul were Jews, and the Old Testament is the Hebrew Bible. Christians and Jews share the Scriptures, the one God, the patriarchs and the prophets. They part on whether Jesus is the Messiah. Paul wrote with deep sorrow about his own people, and insisted that God has not rejected them: "I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not!" (Romans 11:1). The history of Christian contempt for Jews is among the darkest parts of the church's story, and led to centuries of persecution. In 1965 the Catholic Church, in the declaration Nostra Aetate, rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt for the crucifixion and condemned anti-Semitism, and many Protestant churches have said similar things.

Islam arose in the seventh century. Muslims believe in one God, in prophets, in revealed books and in a day of judgment, and they honor Jesus, called Isa, as a prophet born of the virgin Mary. Christians and Muslims agree on much, and disagree on some of the central questions. Muslims deny that Jesus is the Son of God, that God is a Trinity, and that Jesus was crucified, a point on which the Qur'an says that he was not killed or crucified. Christians hold that these are the heart of the gospel. Arabic-speaking Christians have used Allah as the word for God for many centuries.

The apostles' model is to speak with conviction and courtesy. Paul in Athens began from what the people knew and said that God "commands all people everywhere to repent." Peter says to be ready to give a reason for hope, and to "respond with gentleness and respect." Real conversation requires listening, learning what others believe in their own words, and being honest about where we differ.

The Old Testament contains stories of war and of commands to destroy whole peoples, especially the conquest of Canaan in Deuteronomy and Joshua. Many readers, Christian and not, find them disturbing, and the church has never thought they should not be. A few observations help, though they do not remove the difficulty.

First, the Bible gives a reason. Long before the conquest, God told Abraham that his descendants would have to wait because "the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete" (Genesis 15:16). Leviticus says that the nations had defiled themselves and the land, and that the land would vomit them out. Deuteronomy adds that the Israelites should not think it was because of their own goodness: "It is not because of your righteousness or uprightness of heart that you are going in to possess their land" (Deuteronomy 9:5). Canaanite religion included, according to the text, burning children as sacrifices (Deuteronomy 12:31). The conquest is described as a judgment, and one that Israel itself was told it would suffer if it did the same.

Second, the language may be more stylized than it first appears. Joshua 10:40 says that Joshua left no survivors in the whole region, yet the book of Judges, shortly after, records that many of the peoples were still there (Judges 1:21). Ancient writers regularly used sweeping language about victories, and some scholars suggest that the commands to destroy were aimed mainly at the cities and military centers.

Third, Christians read the whole Bible in the light of Christ. Jesus told his disciples to love their enemies and put away the sword, and the New Testament never treats the conquest as a model for the church. Some theologians speak of progressive revelation: that God worked with a people in a violent age and led them step by step toward his full character as seen in Jesus.

Still, some difficulties remain, and honest believers admit them. The best response is not a glib answer, but the trust that the God who is shown in the cross is good, and that one day we will understand.
god-and-violence-in-the-old-testament.q: What do you do with a passage you cannot defend and cannot ignore?

b: This is the hardest question anyone asks about faith, and an honest answer starts by saying so. The old form of it, often credited to the Greek philosopher Epicurus, goes like this: if God is all-good, he would want to stop evil; if he is all-powerful, he could; yet evil exists, so either he is not good or he is not powerful. The argument has force, and Christians have never treated it lightly.

Several answers have been offered, and most thoughtful Christians use more than one. The free will defense, held by Augustine and developed by the philosopher Alvin Plantinga in the 1970s, says that God made people free to love, and that real love requires the freedom to refuse it. A world with free creatures can have the evil they choose. A second view, associated with the second-century bishop Irenaeus and in modern times with John Hick, holds that this world is a place for growth, where character is formed through difficulty. A third looks to the Bible's story: evil entered through the fall, creation itself is "subjected to futility," and God is at work to undo it (Romans 8:20).

The book of Job is the Bible's longest reflection on the question, and its answer is surprising. Job's friends offer neat explanations, and God says that they are wrong. When God finally speaks, he does not explain Job's suffering. He asks him, "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" (Job 38:4). The point is not that Job's pain does not matter, but that there is more to the world than he can see, and that God is present in it.

The most distinctive Christian answer is not an argument, but an event. God did not stay at a distance. In Jesus he entered suffering, was betrayed and killed, and he cried out, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" The Bible does not say that every pain has a visible reason. It says that God has shared it, that he will end it, and that "what you intended against me for evil, God intended for good" even where we cannot yet see how.
if-god-is-good-why-is-there-suffering.q: Which answer to this question has helped you most, and which has hurt?

b: Doubt can feel like the opposite of faith, and many sincere Christians are ashamed of it. The Bible gives a more generous picture.

Some of its heroes doubt. Thomas said that he would not believe the resurrection unless he saw the nail marks, and eight days later Jesus appeared and said, "Put your finger here and look at My hands" (John 20:27). He did not rebuke him, and Thomas answered with the strongest confession in the Gospels, "My Lord and my God!" John the Baptist, in prison, sent messengers to ask Jesus, "Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?" (Matthew 11:3). Jesus answered by pointing to what he was doing, and then praised John. The author of Psalm 73 almost lost his footing when he saw the wicked prosper, until he went to the sanctuary and understood. And the father of a sick boy said what many have said since: "I do believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24). Jesus healed the boy.

The New Testament even tells the church how to treat doubters: "have mercy on those who doubt" (Jude 1:22). It is worth distinguishing different kinds. Some doubt is a question honestly asked, and it is often a sign of a mind that is taking faith seriously. The poet Tennyson wrote in 1850, "There lives more faith in honest doubt, believe me, than in half the creeds." Other doubt comes from hurt, from exhaustion or from avoiding something God asks. And some is a settled refusal to believe, which is unbelief rather than doubt.

What helps is to bring the doubt into the open, to say it to God as the psalmists did, and to talk to a trusted friend or pastor. It helps to keep doing what faith does, praying, reading and meeting with other believers, even when we do not feel anything. It helps to remember that faith is a relationship and not a feeling, and that it rests on the faithfulness of God, which does not depend on how strong ours is.
is-it-all-right-to-doubt.q: What is one doubt you have been afraid to say aloud, and who could you tell?

b: People have offered arguments for the existence of God for as long as there has been philosophy. Christians differ about how far they should lean on them. The Bible rarely argues for God's existence. It assumes it, and says that "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 14:1), and that God's "eternal power and divine nature" can be seen in what he has made (Romans 1:20). Still, thoughtful believers have found the arguments worth considering, and thoughtful skeptics have found them worth disputing.

The cosmological arguments begin with the fact that the universe exists and ask why. Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, offered five ways, several of which argue that a chain of causes cannot go back forever and must have a first cause that is not itself caused. The version called the kalam argument, from medieval Islamic thought, points out that the universe seems to have had a beginning, which fits the Big Bang model, first proposed by a Belgian priest and physicist, Georges Lemaître. Skeptics reply that science may yet explain the beginning without God, or that the question of why anything exists may have no answer.

The design arguments, such as William Paley's watchmaker in 1802, point to the order and complexity of nature. Their modern form is the observation that the basic constants of physics seem finely tuned for life. Critics respond that evolution explains biological design, or that there may be many universes. The moral argument says that objective right and wrong make best sense if there is a moral lawgiver, as C. S. Lewis argued. And many point to the sense of awe, beauty and meaning that is hard to explain on purely material grounds.

Each of these has strong defenders and strong critics, and none is a proof in the sense that a mathematical theorem is. They are better understood as pointers, which make belief reasonable without forcing it. The Bible says that "anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him" (Hebrews 11:6), and promises, "You will seek Me and find Me when you search for Me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13).

A popular story says that science and religion have always been at war, with faith in retreat. Historians of science have largely abandoned that account. The "conflict thesis" was made popular in the late nineteenth century by two books, one by John William Draper in 1874 and one by Andrew Dickson White in 1896, and has been picked apart by later scholars. The real story is more varied.

Christianity helped give rise to modern science. Many of its founders were devout Christians who saw their work as studying God's creation. Johannes Kepler said he was "thinking God's thoughts after him." Isaac Newton wrote more on theology than on physics. Robert Boyle, Michael Faraday and James Clerk Maxwell were all believers. The idea that the universe is orderly and can be understood, because it was made by a rational God, was one of the supports on which the scientific revolution stood. The psalmist said, "Great are the works of the LORD; they are pondered by all who delight in them" (Psalm 111:2).

The Galileo affair of 1633 is often cited as proof of conflict, but its history is complicated. Galileo's case involved politics, personalities and a dispute over scriptural interpretation, and many of the scholars who opposed him did so on scientific grounds shared by astronomers at the time.

There are real points of tension, and the main ones concern how to read Genesis and how to think about evolution. Christians hold several views. Some read Genesis 1 as describing six ordinary days, and hold that the earth is young. Others accept the scientific dating of the universe at about 13.8 billion years and of the earth at about 4.5 billion, and read the days as ages or as a literary framework. Some accept evolution as the means God used, as Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project, does; others reject it. The Big Bang theory was first proposed by Georges Lemaître, a Catholic priest.

The most helpful distinction is between how and why. Science asks how things work, and faith asks why there is anything and what it is for. When both stay in their lane, they can enrich each other, and the psalmist's line holds: "The heavens declare the glory of God."
If Jesus is the only way to the Father, what happens to the people who have never heard of him? It is a serious question, and Christians have answered in three main ways, each with Bible support.

Exclusivism holds that salvation is found only through faith in Christ, and that those who have not heard cannot be saved by other means. It points to Jesus' words, "No one comes to the Father except through Me" (John 14:6), and Peter's, that there is no other name by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). And it points to Paul's questions in Romans: "How then can they call on the One in whom they have not believed? And how can they believe in the One of whom they have not heard?" (Romans 10:14). This is the reason for the urgency of mission.

Inclusivism holds that Christ is the only Savior, but that people may be saved by him without having heard of him, if they respond in faith to the light that they have. It notes that Paul says that the Gentiles who do not have the law show that "the work of the law is written on their hearts" (Romans 2:15), and that Peter says that God welcomes "those from every nation who fear Him and do what is right" (Acts 10:35). Old Testament figures like Melchizedek and Job had faith without knowing the name of Jesus. The Catholic Church's Vatican II said in 1964 that those who through no fault of their own do not know the gospel, but seek God, may reach salvation. C. S. Lewis took a similar view in his last Narnia book.
A third view, universalism, holds that in the end all will be saved. A few Christians have held this, but it has been generally rejected in the church because of the warnings of Jesus.

What all agree on is the character of the Judge. Abraham asked, "Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?" (Genesis 18:25), and the Bible's answer is yes. Christians are told to take the good news to everyone, and not to presume to know who will be saved, trusting that God is both just and merciful.
what-about-those-who-have-never-heard.q: How does the thought of people who have never heard the gospel shape the way you pray?

b: Many people who believe, and many who are searching, share a feeling that God is hard to find. He does not appear, he does not answer on demand, and sometimes he seems absent just when he is needed most. The Bible knows this experience well, and it does not deny it.

The prophet Isaiah says, "Truly You are a God who hides Himself, O God of Israel, the Savior" (Isaiah 45:15). The Psalms are full of the complaint. "How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me?" (Psalm 13:1). "Why, O LORD, do You stand far off? Why do You hide in times of trouble?" (Psalm 10:1). One psalm, number 88, ends without any word of hope: "darkness is my closest companion." It is in the Bible, which tells us that this kind of prayer is permitted. Job asked questions for chapters, and Jesus himself on the cross felt forsaken.

Christian writers have offered several thoughts. One is that God's hiddenness leaves room for freedom, since a God who was overwhelmingly obvious would leave no room for trust or for love that is freely given. Another is that a hidden God is one we are meant to seek, and the promise is that those who seek will find. A third is that his presence is often found in unexpected places, in the weak, the poor and the suffering, and in the cross itself. A fourth is that the silence is sometimes ours: we are not listening or we are distracted.

The sixteenth-century Spanish mystic John of the Cross called the experience "the dark night of the soul," a time when the usual sense of God's nearness falls away, and he held that it can be a stage of deeper growth. Paul says, "we walk by faith, not by sight" (2 Corinthians 5:7). Faith that is tested in darkness is not necessarily weaker. Many have found that God was nearer than they thought, only unseen.
why-does-god-seem-hidden.q: When have you felt that God was silent, and what did you do?

b: Everyone who prays has prayed for something that did not happen. A healing that did not come, a relationship that did not mend, a door that stayed shut. The Bible does not give a single explanation, but it does give several that hold together.

First, the Bible shows that unanswered prayers can come from good people. Paul prayed three times to have a thorn in his flesh removed, and the answer was no: "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). Jesus himself prayed in Gethsemane, "Take this cup from Me," and added, "Yet not what I will, but what You will" (Mark 14:36). The cup did not pass. The answer to a prayer can be no, and the Son of God was given it.

Second, the Bible says that the answer is sometimes yes, sometimes no and sometimes wait. Prayer is not a mechanism that gives what we ask. It is a relationship with a Father who knows better than we do. John says that "If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us" (1 John 5:14). The focus is on his will. James is blunt that some prayers go unanswered because of wrong motives: "you ask with wrong motives, that you may squander it on your pleasures" (James 4:3).

Third, we often do not know what to pray. Paul says, "we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words" (Romans 8:26). There is a prayer going on beneath our own that is always in line with God's will.

Fourth, the Psalms give permission to keep praying through silence. Many of them repeat "How long?" and keep going. Jesus told a parable about a widow who kept asking an unjust judge, to teach that we should pray and not lose heart.

None of this makes the pain of a silent heaven go away, but it can change how we hear it. An unanswered prayer is not proof that God does not care. It may be a place where he is doing something we cannot see yet.
why-doesnt-god-answer-my-prayer.q: Is there a prayer you stopped praying because it seemed unanswered, and would you pray it again?

b: The Bible was written in a world run mostly by men, and it speaks about women with a variety of voices. A fair account shows both the honor it gave them and the questions it still raises.

In the Old Testament, women lead and speak for God. Miriam is called a prophet. Deborah was a prophet and a judge who led Israel and gave a victory (Judges 4:4). Huldah, a prophet in Jerusalem, was consulted by King Josiah's officials when the Book of the Law was found (2 Kings 22:14). Esther saved her people, and Ruth is an ancestor of Jesus. The book of Proverbs ends with a poem about a woman of strength who runs a household and does business.

Jesus broke many conventions. He taught women, which rabbis did rarely, and women traveled with him and supported his work, including Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna (Luke 8:1-3). Mary sat at his feet as a disciple while Martha worked, and he defended her. Women were at the cross and were the first witnesses of the resurrection.

In the early church, women appear as workers and leaders. Priscilla and her husband Aquila taught Apollos, and she is often named first. Phoebe is called a servant, or deacon, of the church at Cenchrea. Paul greets Junia and Andronicus as "outstanding among the apostles" (Romans 16:7), though scholars debate whether this means that they were apostles or well known to the apostles. Lydia led a household church in Philippi.

The difficult passages are 1 Timothy 2:12, "I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man," and 1 Corinthians 14:34 to 35. Christians read them differently. Complementarians hold that they establish a pattern in which certain roles of church leadership are reserved for men. Egalitarians hold that they addressed local situations, and that the whole sweep of Scripture, including Galatians 3:28, affirms the full equality of men and women in ministry. Both groups hold that men and women are equally made in God's image and equally saved.
